findings.summary: The deck stops mid-vendoring: `go mod vendor` is introduced but vendor mode is never explained, and the build-tags chapter the caption promises never appears.
findings.evidence: The final block of page 10 is "Records paths, versions, `## explicit`, go lines / Checked against `go.mod`; a stale mismatch fails the build" — nothing follows. Yet the caption says "Ten pages on go.mod internals, pseudo-versions, semantic import versioning, MVS, the checksum database, replace/retract, vendoring and build tags."
findings.fix: Either add the remaining pages (vendor-mode activation and `-mod=vendor`/`-mod=mod`, pros/cons, then the Build Tags and Workflow/Cheat-Sheet chapters from the syllabus), or cut the vendoring stub from page 10 and edit the caption to list only what the deck actually teaches.

findings.summary: The caption promises coverage of vendoring and build tags, but no page title covers either topic.
findings.evidence: Caption: "Ten pages on go.mod internals, pseudo-versions, semantic import versioning, MVS, the checksum database, replace/retract, vendoring and build tags." — the ten titles end at "replace, exclude, retract, Workspaces" with no vendoring or build-tag page.
findings.fix: Replace "vendoring and build tags" with topics the pages actually cover, e.g. "...the checksum database, replace/retract and workspaces."

findings.summary: The claim that bare `go mod init` infers the module path from the VCS remote is false — Go never reads a git remote to determine a module path.
findings.evidence: code block: "go mod init                # infers the path" / "# from the VCS remote or old vendor config"
findings.fix: Replace the comment with what `findModulePath` actually does: infer only from a package's import comment or from the directory's location under `$GOPATH/src`; otherwise it fails with `cannot determine module path for source directory ... (outside GOPATH, module path must be specified)`. (`.git/config` is only used to print a hint suggesting you run `go mod init <path>`, and legacy vendoring-tool config inference is gone from current toolchains.)

findings.summary: The acronym MVS is used twice on page 3 to explain requirements and `// indirect`, but it is not expanded or defined until page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "`require` names a module at a MINIMUM version" / "Never a pin, never a maximum — MVS may pick higher" and sidebox "Why `// indirect` Appears": "MVS bumped it above what its parent asked for". findings.summary: The v0 page depends on two concepts introduced only later — the `/vN` major-version-in-path rule (page 5/6) and pseudo-versions (page 5).
findings.evidence: Page 4 bullets: "No `/v0` or `/v1` suffix ever exists in a path" and "Parking at v0 dodges the `/vN` rule for v2+"; tip: "An untagged repo forces every consumer onto a pseudo-version." The `/vN` rule is first stated at the end of page 5 ("Major 2 and above must appear in the module path") and pseudo-versions are defined on page 5 ("synthetic version for an untagged commit").
findings.fix: Move the "SemVer Rules & the v0 Escape Hatch" page to after "Semantic Import Versioning" (i.e. after page 6), or keep it here and strip the forward references: drop the `/vN` bullet and rephrase the tip as "An untagged repo forces consumers onto a synthetic version string derived from a commit hash (page 5)".

findings.summary: Saying the `go` line is "NOT a minimum" contradicts current semantics (and the callout directly beneath it): since Go 1.21 the directive is a hard minimum toolchain requirement.
findings.evidence: bullet: "It is NOT a minimum runtime version", immediately followed by callout "Hard Since 1.21 — A newer `go` line makes an older toolchain refuse to build"
findings.fix: Change to "It IS a minimum toolchain requirement (hard since 1.21) — not a constraint on whoever runs your compiled binary"; go.dev/doc/toolchain: "Go 1.21 changed the `go` line to be a mandatory requirement instead."

findings.summary: `go mod tidy` is relied on across four pages as a known command but is never defined anywhere in the deck.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "Comments after directives survive `go mod tidy`"; page 8: "`(main module does not need X)` = tidy will drop it" and "run `go mod tidy -go=1.22` so the graph matches". No block states what tidy does; the syllabus definition ("adds every missing requirement and removes every unused one") lives in the uncovered Workflow chapter.
findings.fix: Add a one-line definition at the first mention on page 3 — e.g. a bullet "`go mod tidy` adds every missing requirement and drops every unused one" — before relying on tidy's behaviour on pages 8 and 10.

findings.summary: The pseudo-version shape given for a pre-release base version drops the pre-release identifier, so it does not match the documented form.
findings.evidence: table row: ["a prerelease","`v1.2.3-0.<ts>-<hash>`"]
findings.fix: Use the documented form `vX.Y.Z-pre.0.<ts>-<hash>` (go.dev/ref/mod: "`vX.Y.Z-pre.0.yyyymmddhhmmss-abcdefabcdef` is used when the base version is a pre-release version like `vX.Y.Z-pre`") — e.g. show `v1.2.3-pre.0.<ts>-<hash>` for base tag `v1.2.3-pre`.

findings.summary: Stating that `@latest` never selects a pre-release is wrong: pre-releases are only deprioritized, and `@latest` resolves to the highest pre-release when no release tags exist.
findings.evidence: bullet: "Prereleases are never chosen by `@latest`" and table row ["`@latest`","highest release tag, no prereleases"]
findings.fix: Reword to "highest release tag; pre-releases only if no release tag exists" — cmd/go's Query doc comment: "the latest available, allowed tagged version, with non-prereleases preferred over prereleases. If there are no tagged versions in the repo, latest returns the most recent commit."

findings.summary: Advising authors to `retract` v1 after shipping v2 misuses retract and contradicts the same tip's "keep v1 alive with fixes".
findings.evidence: callout: "Keep v1 alive with fixes, ship v2 as a new module, then mark v1 `// Deprecated:` and `retract` it."
findings.fix: Drop the `retract` half — retraction marks versions that must not be used (broken/accidental releases) and removes them from `@latest` for existing v1 users. The documented way to signal a superseded major is the module-level `// Deprecated:` comment in v1's `go.mod`.

findings.summary: In the highlighted row of the "Worked Selection" table, the build-list cell renders in pink on the yellow highlight, giving far less contrast than the dark text in the two neighbouring highlighted cells.
findings.evidence: Row "B v1.0.0 | A v1.5.0 | A v1.5.0" — the third cell "A v1.5.0" is drawn in the accent pink (~#e64980) on the yellow highlight (~#f2e26b), roughly a 2.9:1 ratio, while "B v1.0.0" and "A v1.5.0" in the same row use near-black text.
findings.fix: Force highlighted table rows to use the dark on-highlight text colour for inline code/version spans too, so the pink accent is overridden inside a highlight background.

findings.summary: The claim that a published local-path `replace` "breaks every consumer" contradicts the sidebox on the same page and overstates the failure mode.
findings.evidence: callout: "Publishing a library that carries a local-path `replace` breaks every consumer of it." vs sidebox: "Replaces inside a library are ignored downstream"
findings.fix: State the real mechanism: the replace is silently ignored downstream, so consumers resolve the original `require` line — which fails only when that line is a placeholder such as `v0.0.0-00010101000000-000000000000`, and otherwise silently builds against the unreplaced module.
